figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: AnyGameRenderer turns crude gameplay into polished game visuals. Top: one checkpoint handles diverse genres and input types, and renders one input in many styles. Insets show the crude input. Bottom: an agent writes the game and the engine outputs a blockout, which AnyGameRenderer renders into the final visuals. This allows style switching and skips modeling, texturing and animation.
figures.headline: One checkpoint re-renders crude gameplay from many genres and input types into several prompted styles, frame-aligned with the input.
citing_sentences: As shown in Figure 1, AnyGameRenderer takes a crude gameplay recording and a text prompt (optionally with a style anchor image), and outputs the same gameplay re-rendered in the prompted style, frame-aligned with the input.

As illustrated in Figure 1, AnyGameRenderer generalizes across a wide range of genres, including tower defense, auto-battlers, top-down survivors, turn-based battles, kart racing, crowd runners, arena survival, co-op games, and shooters.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Overview of AnyGameRenderer. (a) Paired data from three sources. Agent-made games use multi-stream rendering, which pairs each game render with several aligned crude streams such as blockouts and semantic maps. Unreal Engine scenes use two-stream rendering, which pairs a full render with blockouts. Real gameplay recordings are converted into blockouts by detecting 3D bounding boxes. (b) One training sample: the crude clip is the input video <Video 1>, the target’s first frame serves as an optional anchor, and a six-segment caption defines which real entity each crude shape represents and what must be preserved. (c) Text, <Video 1>, anchor, and noisy target tokens form one sequence for the frozen MiniMax-H3 DiT. Only the LoRA adapters on self-attention and feed-forward layers are trained, and the model renders the input gameplay in the prompted style.
figures.headline: Three data sources feed a frozen video model with a LoRA, which renders crude input video in the style set by the prompt.
citing_sentences: AnyGameRenderer treats game rendering as reference-conditioned video editing: given a crude gameplay recording (a plain reference video) and a caption saying what each crude entity stands for, it generates the same gameplay in a target style (Figure 2).

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Three failures of the zero-shot base model. Red dashed boxes mark the errors. Left: input primitives are left unrendered; the cyan cylinders stay in the output instead of becoming characters. Middle: the input has only two blocks, but the model adds an extra creature that does not exist in the input. Right: the input is a top-down view, but the model renders a frontal group shot.
figures.headline: The zero-shot base model leaves primitives unrendered, adds an extra creature, and turns a top-down view into a frontal shot.
citing_sentences: Rather than collecting generic gameplay, we script scenes around the zero-shot failures (see examples in Figure 3) to ensure entity correspondence:

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Zero-shot MiniMax-H3 versus AnyGameRenderer on held-out cases, with the same seed, steps, and caption. The zero-shot model leaves crude shapes unrendered (rows 1–4), drops the input viewpoint for out-of-domain styles (rows 5–6: a top-down blockout becomes a frontal anime scene or a first-person voxel scene), and adds caption-named characters although the input has only two blocks (row 7). AnyGameRenderer fixes all three. For rows 5–6, the “GT” column is the original in-domain render and serves only as a layout reference.
figures.headline: The zero-shot model leaves crude shapes unrendered and drops the input viewpoint, while AnyGameRenderer keeps both on the same held-out cases.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Entity-sync metrics by genre. Zero-shot MiniMax-H3 (orange) versus AnyGameRenderer (blue) on the held-out benchmark, grouped into first-person shooter, top-down, third-person, crowd, and vehicle games.
figures.headline: AnyGameRenderer raises temporal match over the zero-shot model in every genre, and top-down games stay hardest for both.
citing_sentences: A single checkpoint handles all five genres in our benchmark: first-person shooters, top-down, third-person, crowd, and vehicle games (Figure 5).

abstract: AI coding agents can now build small playable games in minutes, but the results usually look like programmer art: gray blockouts, colored geometric primitives, and flat semantic blobs. We present AnyGameRenderer, a video-to-video generative renderer that turns such footage into high-quality visuals with characters, motion detail, and effects. Throughout, it keeps the layout, camera, and every entity’s position and timing intact. Our AnyGameRenderer generalizes across a wide range of genres that agents build, such as tower defense, auto-battlers, top-down survivors, turn-based battles, kart racing, and crowd runners. AnyGameRenderer takes plain video as its game-state input, with no complex representations such as engine G-buffers, per-object class labels, or low-poly proxies. Gray blockouts, colored primitives, semantic maps, and wireframes all work as input. It also preserves entity correspondence: group counts stay correct, and entities appear and disappear on the right frame. We implement AnyGameRenderer by LoRA fine-tuning MiniMax-H3 ref2va, a 33B reference-video-conditioned video generation model. Training uses $\sim$10k paired clips from three sources: (i) multi-stream rendering data from 38 agent-made games; (ii) two-stream rendering data from Unreal Engine, with programmatically controlled crowds, count changes, and entity scales; and (iii) real gameplay recordings, with pairs reconstructed via 3D-box detection. To evaluate the entity correspondence, we propose an entity-level benchmark of 59 held-out cases with 753 entities, scored against ground-truth boxes. Compared with the base model, AnyGameRenderer better preserves entity correspondence: temporal match rises from 50.9% to 62.9%, missed count changes fall from 34.7% to 21.3%, and fewer entities are hallucinated or left unrendered.

sections.body: The paper targets game footage from AI coding agents, which often has gray blockouts and colored primitives. AnyGameRenderer takes a plain crude video and a text prompt, then outputs the same gameplay in the prompted style, frame-aligned with the input. It is trained on 10,330 paired clips from three sources. The authors also introduce a 59-case entity-level benchmark. Compared with the zero-shot base model, temporal match rises from 50.9% to 62.9%, position match from 57.1% to 61.9%, the unrendered rate falls from 4.1% to 2.9%, and the hallucination rate falls from 52.1% to 46.0%.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Crude game footage can be re-rendered in a chosen style while keeping every entity's count, position and timing.

sections.body: The related work covers language-model game generation, interactive world models that replace the game engine, and generative rendering systems such as CWM, PWM, Matrix-Game 4.0, StreamRender-H3 and SolarRenderer. The authors state that these systems are mostly shown on third-person, driving or self-built 3D scenes, and that many depend on a fixed intermediate representation. They also argue that frame-level metrics barely change when a small entity is missing or a group arrives late, and that edge agreement can reward leaving crude blocks unrendered. The paper therefore makes correspondence the main target of both training data and evaluation.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Earlier systems rely on fixed intermediate representations, and none measures entity-level correspondence.

sections.body: The method treats rendering as reference-conditioned video editing. The crude clip is passed as the reference video, and a six-segment caption states which real entity each crude shape represents and what must be preserved. A rank-128 LoRA is trained on all transformer blocks with the flow-matching objective, while the base weights stay frozen. Training uses a global batch size of 16, clips of 124 frames at 24 fps, and 16 NVIDIA H200 GPUs. Three epochs over all 10,330 clips take about 48 hours. Inference uses 20-step Euler sampling, and a LoRA multiplier of 0.7 is recommended for out-of-domain text-only styles.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: A rank-128 LoRA on MiniMax-H3 is trained with a six-segment caption that fixes which crude shapes are entities.

sections.body: Each source gives crude and styled videos that share camera and layout and are frame-aligned by construction. Agent-made games contribute 3,221 clips with primitive, coarse, semantic and depth passes. Unreal Engine scenes contribute 3,910 clips; they script same-color groups of 2 to 20 characters that spawn or despawn mid-clip, entity sizes from 20 to 600 pixels, and mixed camera views. Real recordings contribute 3,199 clips, with detected 3D boxes rendered as solid, wireframe, cylinder and ellipsoid proxies. Table 1 gives the mixture, which the authors describe as roughly equal weight, about 14.8 hours of video.
sections.heading: Data
sections.headline: Training pairs come from 38 agent-made games, scripted Unreal Engine scenes and real recordings, totaling 10,330 clips.

sections.body: The benchmark has 59 cases with 753 annotated entities: 11 two-stream Unreal Engine cases, 14 real recordings and 34 multi-stream cases. Entities in the generated video are found with SAM3 segmentation, linked into tracks, and matched to input boxes per frame with the Hungarian method. Four main metrics are reported: temporal match, position match, unrendered rate and hallucination rate. Across all cases, on-time appearance rises from 55.9% to 67.6%, and never-appear falls from 26.0% to 20.2%. Gains are largest on two-stream cases, where temporal match reaches 96.6% against a GT floor of 98.5%. Real recordings improve least: temporal match rises from 46.5% to 51.1%, and missed count changes stay at 20.0%. The hallucination rate rises slightly on top-down and third-person games.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: On 59 held-out cases, temporal match rises from 50.9% to 62.9% and missed count changes fall from 34.7% to 21.3%.

sections.body: The conclusion restates the contribution: a single LoRA on MiniMax-H3, trained on paired data from agent-made games, Unreal Engine two-stream rendering and real gameplay recordings. The checkpoint takes plain video, from gray blockouts and colored primitives to semantic maps and wireframes, and keeps entities in sync with the input. On the held-out benchmark, temporal match rises from 50.9% to 62.9%, and missed count changes fall from 34.7% to 21.3%. The authors state that a general renderer that keeps every entity in place could help agent-made games look as good as they play.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The renderer keeps entities in sync across genres and crude input types, with gains shown on one held-out benchmark.
